k01: git push --force-with-lease overwrites the remote branch only if it still points where your last fetch saw it, so you never clobber a teammate's commits the way a plain force push can.
k02: a detached HEAD means you checked out a commit directly instead of a branch; new commits made there have no branch pointing at them, so create one with git switch -c before they get lost.
k03: git rm --cached removes a file from the index so git stops tracking it while leaving the working copy on disk; add the path to .gitignore afterwards so it does not come back.
k04: ECONNREFUSED means the tcp connection was actively rejected: nothing is listening on that host and port. check that the server process actually started, that the port number matches, and whether it binds to localhost only.
k05: a 502 bad gateway means a proxy or load balancer contacted the upstream server and got an invalid response or none at all; check whether the backend process is up and the proxy's upstream configuration points at the right address.
k06: http 429 too many requests is rate limiting; the Retry-After header tells the client how many seconds to wait before retrying, so honor it and back off instead of hammering the endpoint.
k07: SIGTERM asks a process to shut down and can be caught for cleanup, while SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored and the kernel terminates the process immediately; kill -9 sends SIGKILL.
k08: lsof -i :8080 lists which process holds the port open; read the pid from the output and stop or kill that process to free the port for your server.
k09: tail -f follows a file as it grows, printing each new line as it is appended, which is the standard way to watch a log file live in the terminal.
k10: chmod 755 grants the owner read, write and execute while group and others get read and execute; each digit is an octal bitmask of the rwx permission bits.
k11: OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated the process, exit code 137; raise the memory limit or shrink the workload's footprint.
k12: docker compose reads a yaml file that declares services, images, ports, volumes and networks, and docker compose up starts the whole stack with one command.
k13: python -m venv creates an isolated virtual environment with its own interpreter and site-packages; activate it so pip installs land inside the project instead of the system python.
k14: the global interpreter lock lets only one thread execute python bytecode at a time, so threads cannot speed up cpu-bound code; use multiprocessing for parallelism and threads for io waiting.
k15: async def defines a coroutine and await suspends it until the awaited operation completes, letting the event loop run other tasks meanwhile; asyncio.run drives the top-level coroutine.
k16: the n+1 query problem is one query for a list plus one more query per row for its related records; fix it with a join or eager loading so the data arrives in a single round trip.
k17: EXPLAIN shows the query plan the database chose: scan types, join order and index usage. a sequential scan over a large table where you expected an index lookup is the usual finding.
k18: store passwords with a slow adaptive hash like bcrypt or argon2 and a per-password salt; the work factor makes brute force expensive, and fast hashes like plain sha256 are not enough.
k19: a jwt is three base64url sections, header, payload and signature; the payload is only encoded, not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can decode and read the claims. the signature only proves it was not altered.
k20: catastrophic backtracking happens when nested or overlapping quantifiers force the regex engine to try exponentially many ways to match, so a long non-matching input hangs the process; rewrite the pattern so alternatives cannot overlap.
p01: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit while keeping everything you wrote staged in the index, so no work is lost.
p02: the reflog records every position HEAD has held; run git reflog to find the hash from before the reset and reset back to it, recovering commits that looked destroyed.
p03: git stash shelves your uncommitted changes and leaves a clean working tree; switch to the other branch, and later git stash pop restores the shelved work.
p04: long-running javascript blocks the main thread, so rendering and input freeze; move the heavy computation into a web worker so the ui thread stays responsive.
p05: use asyncio: create the request coroutines and run them together with asyncio.gather, so each one waits on the network without blocking the others.
p06: that is cors: the browser blocks cross-origin requests unless the server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, and a preflight OPTIONS request has to succeed first.
p07: set a timeout on the request so a silent server fails fast instead of hanging forever; most http clients take a timeout parameter and raise an error once it expires.
p08: du -sh on each directory shows which ones are largest, and df -h shows filesystem usage overall; drill downward with du until you find what is eating the disk.
p09: kill sends SIGTERM first to allow a clean shutdown; if the process ignores it, kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, and the kernel removes the process.
p10: memoize it: cache the result keyed by the function's arguments and return the cached value on repeated calls; python's functools.lru_cache does this with one decorator.
p11: mount a volume: docker volumes live outside the container's filesystem, so the data survives when the container is removed or recreated.
p12: order the dockerfile so installing dependencies is its own layer before the source code is copied in; docker caches layers, so unchanged dependency files let the install step be reused instead of re-run on every build.
p13: use a multi-stage build: compile in a full build image, then copy only the finished artifacts into a slim or alpine base image so the final image stays small and pulls quickly.
p14: issue a signed token such as a jwt at login; every request carries it and the server verifies the signature locally instead of looking up a session in the database.
p15: that is cross-site scripting, xss: user input rendered into the page as html lets an attacker run script in the visitor's browser; escape output on render and set a content security policy.
p16: revoke and rotate the key immediately and treat it as compromised; scrubbing it from history is not enough because clones, forks and caches keep copies, so rotation is the real fix.
p17: add an index on the columns the lookup filters by; without one the database scans the entire table, and the scan time grows with the row count.
p18: wrap both updates in a transaction: begin, run the two updates, commit; if either fails, rollback undoes the other so the database never shows a half-applied state.
p19: default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time, so a mutable default like a list is shared across every call; use None as the default and create a fresh list inside the body.
p20: iterate over the file object itself: for line in the open file reads lazily one line at a time, so memory use stays flat no matter how large the file is.
